facts.claim: "Prisoner" is track 4 on Stumfol's debut album "12", released 10 June 2013 on Fond Of Life Records. It runs 2:41 on Bandcamp.
Christian Stumfol is credited as the writer and composer of the album's songs, including "Prisoner".

Discogs credits the "12" LP as recorded by Antonio Raimondo, mastered by Arne Thiemann, with layout by Matthias Bäuerle. The vinyl was issued under Fond Of Life (FOL066) and Angry Chuck Records (CHUCK#32).
Antonio Raimondo is listed among the various members and collaborators in the Stumfol project, alongside Christian's brother Daniel Stumfol, Tim Petran and Andreas Streble.
A video for "Prisoner" was released in April 2013, ahead of the album.
The "12" LP came in 12 different hand-screenprinted cover versions, each limited to 25 copies. Twelve different artists made artwork for the album's 12 songs.

Ox-Fanzine said "Prisoner" had circulated online as a video for some time before the album. It described the album as sounding like a mix of Tom Petty and Bruce Springsteen, with Rumbleseat and Foundations also named as reference points.

Allschools said that on tracks like "From Peacetime To War" and "Prisoner", Stumfol keeps things relaxed and uses little frills. It placed the album between best-friends folk, working-class attitude and acoustic punk.
Christian Stumfol is a German singer-songwriter from Baden-Württemberg. He also sings and plays bass in the punk band Clap Your Hands Twice, and "12" was his solo debut album.

The albums that followed "12" were Pareto (2014), Cold Brew (2016) and Long Story Short (2019). Before the album he had released the 7-inch "Coffee Sessions", limited to 100 copies with covers hand-painted in coffee.

research.lineage: Stumfol's songs sit in the punk-rooted singer-songwriter and acoustic-folk tradition, with Springsteen and Tom Petty comparisons from reviewers and a DIY ethos tied to Germany's Fond Of Life Records punk scene.

draft:
The most startling line in **Prisoner** is also the quietest: "No one tried to stop me." The narrator of Christian Stumfol's song spends most of its 2:40 describing a life inside a cell he was born into, a voice in a language he couldn't follow, a light he couldn't tell from a dream. Then he walks out, and nothing happens. No guard, no alarm, no chase. The escape is an anticlimax, and that anticlimax is the whole wound.

Stumfol builds toward it with a refrain that works like a proverb someone repeats to stay sane: "You cannot miss what you have never seen before / But deep inside, you know there must be more." The first line is a defense, a way of making peace with the walls. The second gives the defense away. Both lines sit in the same breath and neither wins, which is exactly what living with a quiet longing feels like. You talk yourself out of it and it stays anyway.

The final verse is where relief and regret arrive together. The narrator learns he was always free, free "as a bird," and you can hear the lift in that discovery. But the song doesn't end on the bird. It ends on a confession, "But I was just too scared to see," and then on the open question of who he could have been. The cage was fear. Finding the door open means admitting he could have left long ago, and the song lets that sting sit next to the joy without smoothing either one over.

The arrangement refuses any drama, which is right for a story whose big moment is nobody reacting. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls out patient arpeggios over a walking bass line, while brushes keep a soft, steady beat on the kit. The tempo is slow and the groove relaxed, almost easy. The voice is clear and mid-range, sung smooth and melodic with no harmonies to lean on, so the words land plainly, one person telling you something hard in a level tone. The production is clean, with nothing between you and the story.

It's a long way from the punk Stumfol plays bass and sings in with Clap Your Hands Twice, but the DIY roots show. "Prisoner" opened his solo debut *12* on Fond Of Life Records, an album that came in twelve hand-screenprinted covers. Ox-Fanzine heard Tom Petty and Springsteen in the record, with Rumbleseat and Foundations as nearer cousins. Allschools singled out this track for its relaxed, low-frills approach and placed the album between best-friends folk, working-class attitude and acoustic punk. That fits: this is a campfire parable told by someone who came up in basements.

The song sticks because it turns the fear of a locked door into something worse and more familiar, the dawning knowledge that you were the one holding it shut.
